name: Tasmanian, south-eastern language, mainland hinterland
confidence_why: Crowley and Dixon 1981, the standard account of Tasmanian phonology, call stress placement its most elusive aspect and conclude only that any syllable but the last can be stressed, and Capell 1968 agrees it cannot be established for a language with no living speakers; the one dissent, Taylor 2006, reads the nineteenth-century recorders' diacritics as showing initial stress but is a preliminary MA thesis that defers its own full account to a morphology not yet.
catalog_citation: Crowley, Terry & R.M.W. Dixon. 1981. Tasmanian. In R.M.W. Dixon & Barry J. Blake (eds), Handbook of Australian Languages, Volume 2, 394-421. Canberra: Australian National University Press. (ANU Open Research scan, hdl:1885/114846)
catalog_locator: Section 2.4 'Stress', p. 413 (the whole section sits on this page, section 2.5 Phonotactics opens p. 414). Scope statement section 2.1, p. 407.
catalog_quote: The position of stress within a word is perhaps the most elusive aspect of Tasmanian phonology. We have the following source material: [a] Walker marks each vowel with either ¯ or ˘; these marks apparently indicate accent rather than quantity (see the comment in Roth 1899, p.1 of Appendix). [b] Norman uses the same marks, probably in the same way. [c] Milligan says 'when a double consonant or two consonants stand together, the first carries the accent, as in the English words cunningly, peppery, cobbler, pipkin.' This somewhat elusive statement perhaps means that the vowel preceding a sequence of two consonants (in Milligan's orthography) bears stress. [d] Tindale's transcriptions. [e] The Fanny Cochrane Smith recordings. [f] The 1972 Crowley recordings of Mrs. Heffernan and Mrs. Mundy. From these sources it appears that a disyllabic word is always stressed on the first syllable, whereas a trisyllabic word can be stressed on either first or second syllable. Our only general conclusion concerning stress in Tasmanian is thus: any syllable except the last can bear stress.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Philological reconstruction for Tasmanian generally (data mainly mid-eastern and south-eastern): stress never on the final syllable; disyllables are initial-stressed; trisyllables carry stress on the first or the second syllable, with no stated conditioning. Taylor 2006 (pp. 257-259) reads the same records as initial (first word-element) stress; Milligan 1859 p. 282 says the syllable before a written double consonant/cluster 'carries the accent'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated by Crowley & Dixon; Taylor 2006 explicitly denies the mainland-style alternating rhythm for Palawa words.
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the first-or-second-syllable indeterminacy in trisyllables; authors stress the poverty of the evidence (orthographic accent marks of Walker and Norman, Milligan's remark, Tindale, degraded Fanny Cochrane Smith cylinders, 1972 rememberers).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in isolated recorded words (19th-c. wordlists and citation forms on cylinders); statement is for 'Tasmanian' as an areal whole, phonology 'based mainly on the mid-eastern and south-eastern languages' (p. 407), where 'south-eastern' pools Bruny Island (brun1235) with the mainland hinterland (sout1439). No hinterland-specific stress evidence exists: the French primary lists for this variety (Labillardiere 1800, Rossel 1808) say nothing about accent.
new_statements.identity_note: sout1439 is the mainland ('hinterland') half of what Crowley & Dixon 1981 and AIATSIS T5 call 'South-eastern' (Nuenonne: D'Entrecasteaux Channel, Recherche Bay, Huon, Mount Royal); Glottolog, following Bowern, splits it from Bruny Island (brun1235). The quoted statement is made for 'Tasmanian' as a whole; C&D say (p. 407) their phonology 'is based mainly on the mid-eastern and south-eastern languages', and their 'South-eastern' region pools Bruny Island with the hinterland (as does Milligan's column 'Mount Royal, Brune Island, Recherche Bay'). The stress evidence they list (Walker's and Norman's marks, Milligan's note, Tindale, Fanny Cochrane Smith cylinders, 1972 rememberers) is not localised to the hinterland variety, whose own earliest records (Labillardiere 1800, Rossel 1808, Peron 1802) carry no accent information (checked). The same statement already serves tasm1247 and brun1235 in this compilation.
